procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but the FIRs were registered in relation to the state of Gujarat.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The common judgment dated 17.10.2013 passed by the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in Special Criminal Application Nos. 1265, 1266, 1267, 1268, 1269, 2930, 2931, 2932, 2933 and 2934 of 2013.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad allowed applications filed by the respondents under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, and quashed five First Information Reports (FIRs) Nos. 50/2013, 51/2013, 52/2013, 53/2013, and 54/2013, all dated 19th February, 2013.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, feeling aggrieved by the High Court's judgment quashing the FIRs, filed appeals by way of special leave before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's judgment, and effectively reinstated the FIRs.

directions: The impugned judgment is set aside.
The Criminal Applications filed by the accused persons (respondents herein) under Section 482 of the Code out of which these appeals arise are dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the five FIRs.

facts: The accused persons challenged five out of six First Information Reports (FIRs) before the High Court.
The accused argued that the five subsequent FIRs were merely repetitions of the first one, contained overlapping and identical allegations, and were therefore unnecessary.
The High Court accepted this argument, found that the FIRs were based on identical facts, and quashed the five FIRs using its inherent powers.
law: The High Court has inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash FIRs to prevent abuse of the process of court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.
application: The Supreme Court independently reviewed all six FIRs to assess the situation.
After its review, the Supreme Court found itself unable to agree with the reasoning and conclusion of the High Court.

The Court criticized the High Court for conducting an extensive, 46-page factual examination of the FIRs, noting that it had appreciated the allegations "like an Appellate Court," which was inappropriate at that stage.
The Supreme Court concluded that there was "no justifiable reason" for the High Court to have invoked its inherent powers under Section 482 to quash the five FIRs.
The Court deliberately chose not to provide its own detailed reasoning to avoid prejudicing the parties, as the investigation was not yet complete and the trial had not started.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, concluding that the High Court was not justified in quashing the five FIRs. It found no valid reason for the High Court to have used its inherent powers and therefore overturned its judgment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the five FIRs.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, as inferred from the court's agreement, is that the High Court was not justified in quashing the five FIRs because there were significant distinguishing features among the six FIRs, and they were not merely repetitive.
respondent_arguments: The five subsequent FIRs were an abuse of the process of law as they involved an overlapping of offences based on identical allegations, with no substantial changes except for the repetition of words. Therefore, the High Court was correct in quashing them.

cases.case_name: State of West Bengal & Ors. v. Swapan Kumar Guha & Ors.
cases.principle: The Supreme Court relied on the concurring opinion of Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud and Justice A.N. Sen.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is only when on reading the First Information Report (FIR) that no cognizable offence is disclosed, that the High Court may exercise its powers to quash the FIR.
obiter: The parties are at liberty, at an appropriate stage, to move to the High Court with a prayer to club and then transfer all the six cases to one competent Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Upon its own perusal of the six FIRs, the Court found distinguishing factual allegations that were sufficient to repel the challenge made by the accused persons. The Court concluded that all six FIRs are legal and proper, each requiring a full investigation, and therefore the High Court was not justified in quashing five of them.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 482 CrPC, an FIR can only be quashed when on a mere reading of it, a sheer absurdity in the allegations is noticed and when no prima facie cognizable case is made out. A court exercising this power cannot undertake a detailed examination of the facts contained in the FIRs by acting as an Appellate Court.
